The military leaders had ordered that no marches or protests be held in the region. Nevertheless, the Tigray region has recently seen continuous demonstrations. Successive marches have been held in Mekelle, Adigrat, Maychew, Korem, Alamata and other towns. One side of the demonstrations was seen supporting the TPLF of Debretsion (Dr) and the military commanders, chanting slogans such as "Let the decisions of the TPLF and the security force be respected, let the party's legal personality be restored, let the displaced return quickly, let the interim administration be corrected, let the effort to dismantle the army stop." The other side of the peaceful demonstrations was seen supporting the interim administration. With slogans such as "Let the effort to dismantle the government stop, we do not want the army to become the instrument of one group, we support the interim administration, let our land be returned," it spent days supporting the interim administration and opposing the military commanders and the TPLF head office. This demonstration continued until yesterday, and it has been reported that in some areas it led to clashes with security forces in which people were injured.

In the midst of this, Ato Getachew, who appeared on the television screen, made a calming appeal, saying that the security force should not be thrown into turmoil because of the political leadership's problems. The opposition party called Salsay Weyane Tigray, which issued a statement on the matter, condemned the political interference of the military leaders and described the statement that "no protest demonstrations be held" as a Derg-style order. The coalition of parties that includes Arena Tigray and Baytona, in a joint statement, also strongly condemned the political interference of the military leaders.

Ato Gebru Asrat, a veteran Arena party politician and former TPLF fighter, described the recent situation as the occasion on which the Tigray army leaders openly declared their alliance with the TPLF group of Debretsion (Dr). He said he found the military officers' decision to be one with "no legal, institutional or constitutional basis."

"The TPLF group of Debretsion (Dr) is working to oppose and delegitimise the senior army commanders by gathering so-called corps commanders and mid-level commanders who were former TPLF cadres. It is not the top leaders but those below who declared that they stand with the TPLF. The youth, however, understood this and came out to protest. Large peaceful demonstrations have been held in Tigray's towns, including Mekelle. The youth opposed them, saying 'you are Shaebia's errand boys.' What the youth are saying is that even the TPLF's political cadres and leadership are no longer needed for Tigray at this time, and in such a situation they are publicly expressing their anger that the military leaders have abandoned their neutrality, intervened in politics and are striving to bring the TPLF back from the dead," he explained.

"About 200 army leaders gathered. Of these, however, some 25 - senior officers at that - opposed the matter and walked out. From the moment the agenda was set, there were those who said we are servants of the government and should not meddle in politics. There were army commanders who opposed the agenda when it was tabled, saying we should remain neutral from politics, and who stormed out of the meeting just as it was about to be put to a vote. And since the day before yesterday, the military leaders who separately issued a statement saying they support the TPLF have been trying to incriminate these officers who walked out in opposition. Among the 25 officers who walked out are key commanders such as Wedi Ashebir, Wedi Abate and Wedi Antiru. Twelve of them are generals said to hold decisive leadership authority. When the public held protest demonstrations, they made their voice heard even by coming out carrying photographs of these officers who say the armed forces should be neutral. For example, the army unit led by the officer known as Army 44, whom the group of statement-issuing officers decided to expel, went as far as deciding to block roads, saying it would not accept the removal of its leader. It was the force led by Wedi Abate in the north-east area that did this. The armies led by the other twenty-four may also reflect a similar stance, saying 'if our leaders are touched.' The officers' decision that the army must side with the TPLF head office group and stand against the interim administration has itself divided the army's commanders. And this, beyond the popular protest, is also creating a standoff within the armed forces," he said, explaining the recent political polarisation created in Tigray by the decision the army took.

Ato Gebru says the 25 senior army leaders who walked out in opposition to the decision of the military leaders' assembly had, before the corps meeting, clearly decided that they are obedient servants of the government, and he explained that they held meetings for seven days and adopted this position. However, he notes that they entered the meeting when the idea arose of gathering as a corps and taking a decision there. But since many of the army's leaders had chosen to be TPLF cadres, in the end a position statement was tabled for decision holding that the Tigray interim administration is an enemy and must be dissolved so that the legally empowered TPLF takes over responsibility. At that point the 25 top army leaders opposed the decision and walked out of the assembly, he explained to Reporter, recounting the process from its beginning.

The armed force that was known during the northern war as the Tigray Defence Forces (TDF) - its military leaders were among the main negotiators at the time the Pretoria agreement was signed. Following the signing of the peace agreement, when the Tigray interim administration was established, the responsibility for primarily controlling the region's security work was given to a force drawn from this army. The leaders of the Tigray security force were also made forces with their own seat and authority within the Tigray interim administration. Redwan Hussein (Ambassador), one of the main negotiators representing the government at Pretoria, when explaining at that time how the agreement was signed, indicated that although the agreement document contained a provision that no armed force other than the federal security forces could operate in Tigray, the federal government, in good faith and on the grounds that it would benefit the people of Tigray, gave the authority to maintain the region's peace to the Tigray security forces themselves.

Although there is no clause in the agreement preventing the federal defence forces from carrying out peacekeeping work in the region, Redwan (Ambassador) had also said, at a meeting held with opposition political organisations a few days after the agreement was signed, that government representatives, in open discussion with the military and political leaders who came to Pretoria to negotiate on behalf of the TPLF, agreed that it would be better for the Tigray security force itself, rather than the defence forces, to take over Tigray's security matters, and that the responsibility was given on that basis.

The government negotiator explained in detail that although the agreement said the defence forces would take full control of security work, the decision was taken in good faith and by mutual understanding, only because a common understanding had been reached that the full deployment of the defence forces in Tigray and the disarmament of Tigrayan fighters, with the defence forces taking over security work entirely, would, beyond leading to the conclusion that Tigray's political forces had been utterly defeated, not be good for the psychology of the people of Tigray, nor for the next round of political negotiations and mutual understandings, and moreover would not bring lasting peace.

The Tigray interim administration, itself a product of this Pretoria agreement, was established as the "Tigray Region Inclusive Interim Administration" under Council of Ministers Regulation No. 533/2015. It is also mentioned that the interim administration's regulation was issued following the provision set out in Article 62(9) of the Ethiopian Constitution, which stipulates the powers and functions of the House of Federation, stating that when a danger that endangers the constitution and the constitutional order arises in a region, the federal government can be made to intervene. The Tigray Inclusive Interim Administration Regulation also explicitly states that it is based on Proclamation No. 359/95, issued to determine the circumstances in which the federal government intervenes in regional affairs.

As clearly set out in the preamble of the Tigray Inclusive Interim Administration Regulation, it is indicated that the federal government has the power, under Article 14/2(b) of Proclamation No. 539/95, to suspend the regional council and the regional government and establish an interim administration directly accountable to the federal government. In the same regulation it is also stated unambiguously that it is the country's Prime Minister who approves the appointment of the head of the inclusive interim administration to be established in Tigray.

When the TPLF says it negotiated with the government and signed the Pretoria agreement, or that it is the owner of the Pretoria agreement, in legal terms it is understood to have fully accepted these laws and procedures for establishing the Tigray interim administration. As set out in the founding regulation of the Tigray Inclusive Interim Administration, it is clearly indicated that structuring the region's administrative structures and assigning office heads in each place is the task of the interim administration. On this basis, just as a soldier anywhere in the world is obedient to the government, it is also assumed that the region's security force is under the interim administration.

It is said that the TPLF chairman and former president of the Tigray region, Debretsion Gebremichael (Dr), in his own law, Proclamation No. 365/2015, stipulated that government structures, including the security force, are under the regional government. It is also said that the Tigray interim administration, as soon as it was established, took this over and continued it by issuing its own regulation known as Regulation No. 4. Although the fact that the interim administration has full authority to command and deploy the security force has a legal basis, the TPLF under the TPLF head office has repeatedly been seen trying to command the army. For example, on Megabit 27, 2016 E.C., when the group of Debretsion (Dr) issued a statement, it accused the interim administration, saying "it is working to weaken the army and transform itself into a military order," and it called for action to be taken. It is also recalled that when the TPLF of Debretsion (Dr) held its general assembly, it made a call that "the legal TPLF is now me," and that the army should take action against the leaders under the interim administration who trade in its name and hand power over to it. Although it is widely agreed that the interim administration can command the security force under the authority given to it by various laws, on what basis the group holding the TPLF head office claims this authority has been widely disputed.

The head office TPLF has at times been said to bear responsibility for what happens in Tigray because it is a signatory to and owner of the Pretoria agreement. At other times it was said that because the interim administration has not properly exercised the authority given to it, and because the TPLF holds 51 percent of the vote within the interim administration, it can decide not only who is placed in the administration but also the decisions that are taken. Entirely partisan positions have also been echoed, saying that because the TPLF still has a strong and unshakeable social base in Tigray and has built an extensive structure at every level down to the kebele, there can be no force besides it that should be concerned with the matter.

On the other hand, there are also many supporters who say it is appropriate that the officials of the interim administration have reflected a strong position that government and party should not be mixed. Many point out that, given the current concrete political situation in Tigray and taking the legal basis into account, there is no enabling condition for the TPLF to make itself the government or the all-doing commander beyond being one political organisation. Nor are there few who try to argue that the clash between the two forces arose because the TPLF crossed this line and meddled in government work.

Meanwhile, at a time when the claim that the group of Debretsion (Dr) has formed an alliance with Shaebia and won the support of Tigray's military officers is being widely circulated, news that the Brigade Nhamedu group, which opposes the Shaebia government, held a meeting in Addis Ababa has raised many questions. It has also created the worry of whether the matter is crossing over from the TPLF's internal split into a regional conflict.

Ato Gebru, who notes that Shaebia too is supporting this movement of the military leaders, suggests that the TPLF of Debretsion (Dr) has a desire to operate in alliance with Shaebia if possible. Ato Gebru, who notes that the federal government too believes the interim administration is weak, mentions that the former Minister of Defence Abraham Belay (Dr) also confirmed this recently.

Ato Gebru explains that Tigray's political chaos has created multifaceted problems. He indicated that the tension the military officers have now created will, starting from creating a civil war in Tigray, also create a new tension in the alignment of forces with Shaebia as well as with the federal government and other forces. He says the TPLF's old cadres and the many military officers they have now gathered around them do not want the accountability and the demand for change that is coming in Tigray. He also explains that keeping the old political line intact as far as possible has become a matter of life and death for them.

The veteran politician, who suggests that whether the TPLF continues or dies as a party is not a concern for Tigray, shared his worry that if the army digs in, insisting that the TPLF must remain in power, the Tigray crisis will enter a dire condition. He indicated that his own Arena party as well as other opposition parties, civic associations and forces supporting change have taken the position that a new inclusive interim administration should be established in Tigray.

"The TPLF of Debretsion (Dr) and the group of military leaders it has assembled also has a desire to work together with Shaebia. It is trying this in practice, and beyond that it has become known that it has begun efforts to form an alliance with Amhara forces in order to march on Addis Ababa. And Shaebia is known to be a force that is also allied with Egypt," said Ato Gebru, adding that the matter is a tension that goes beyond Tigray and threatens the country.

For his part, Getachew Assefa (Dr), a Tigray political analyst resident in Canada, says that the Brigade Nhamedu meeting in Addis Ababa is an indicator that there are war preparations between Ethiopia and Eritrea.

"The relationship between Shaebia and the TPLF gives much to think about. In 1977 E.C. it was Shaebia that prevented the people of Tigray from finding a way out of the famine. Its differences with the TPLF are deep-rooted. Nevertheless, there are still people in the TPLF today who feel absolute submission to Shaebia. It was one month before the Tigray war began that Shaebia's people wrote a document about the attack they would carry out on Tigray. They decided in advance that Tigray's political elite should have no organisation beyond the Abune Aregawi holy-water association. The document they wrote recently confirms the same. The Shaebians are making good use of the division of Tigray's political elites. Everything inside Tigray is decided by Shaebia. Wedi Beshasha can do nothing; they have concluded that although Debretsion's (Dr) clique has popular support, the interim administration is powerless, and they have prepared Tigray's affairs for their next objective.

The Shaebians, having committed all that destruction on Tigray, find it astonishing to think that the people of Tigray will still stand by their side and support them in fighting the Ethiopian government they call the enemy. No one attempts this except those within the TPLF who are utterly subservient to Shaebia," he explained to Reyot Media.

Semhal Meles, the daughter of the former Prime Minister Meles Zenawi, has recently published an English-language article raising many ideas about Tigray's political tension, given the questioning title "Is the Tigray military force a neutral arbitrator of conflict?" or "Tigray Military Forces: Partial Arbitrator of Conflict?"

Semhal, who sets out by surveying the events since the TPLF began to be split into two camps - one under the interim administration and one under the TPLF head office - notes that no force has emerged that is equally acceptable both to the people of Tigray and to the federal government. One may lack acceptance among the people of Tigray but have acceptance with the federal government. The other may have less acceptance among the people of Tigray but gain higher acceptance with the federal government, she says, examining the political stature of the two groups; Semhal tries to show that the struggle to be found acceptable in both directions is one of the origins of the dispute they have entered. She says that, just as there is the disagreement created by the signing, ownership and implementation of the Pretoria peace agreement, on the other hand the differences over the interim administration's independence and decision-making authority, and over party interference, also contribute to the split. Semhal, who notes that until recently the Tigray army had wavered between the differences of the two groups and struggled not to let its position tilt to one side, states that in the end the army has confirmed that it stands with the side of Debretsion (Dr) and those who lead the TPLF head office, and she details that this, beyond upsetting the alignment of Tigray's political forces, could bring a severe crisis for the region.

Semhal, who presents both the TPLF's split and the army's tilt to one side as linked to the erosion of Tigray's overall political unity, says that given the existential dangers Tigray has faced and still faces, the continuation of the split and the erosion of Tigray's unity brings additional grave danger. Semhal, who says the Prosperity government will continue to aggravate Tigray's problem and fan the fire, notes that the Election Board has been seen dragging out - including by issuing a proclamation - so that it does not easily respond to the demand raised by the group of Debretsion (Dr) that the TPLF's legal recognition be restored. She also says that various delays are being carried out so that the constitutional order is not restored in Tigray, so that an election is not held in Tigray for the region to form its own government, and so that it does not have its own representatives in the federal parliament and the House of Federation. She underlines that this frustrates not only the democratic order but also the effort to build a multinational federal country. She also warns that if Tigray's political elites, seeing the danger coming upon the people of Tigray and the country as a whole, do not devise a solution that guarantees our existence, the outcome will be dangerous.

"Prime Minister Abiy's (Dr) government will not determine the way it handles the conduct of the Tigray army without properly examining the nature of its relationship with the new Donald Trump administration. During Trump's earlier term, America's relationship with Ethiopia hung solely on the favourable attitude Vice President Mike Pence had towards Ethiopia. And Prosperity benefited greatly from this. Be that as it may, Donald Trump is not a leader who has a policy option for African countries, which he insults as filthy. There is no certainty about what his relationship with African countries such as Ethiopia will be based on in his second term. At a time when the violation of international law and order, as well as territorial expansionism, are taking root, the global acceptability of liberalism and capitalism has fallen into danger. Within this global reality, will the Tigrayan elites in whose hands the fate of the people of Tigray lies continue, as they have always done, as promoters of neoliberal politics cloaked in revolutionary democracy, or will they join the political camp that says change and reform should come first? That is a matter to be awaited," she analyses. Finally, she says that unless Tigray's elites enter into seeking political solutions that go with the changing international political situation and that withstand the dangers that have arrived, the existence of the people of Tigray will fall into grave danger, worse than the feared prospect of becoming a people without a country.

At this time, when the dispute created by the TPLF's splitting in two is said to threaten the country, the absence of a response from the federal government is being widely discussed by many. Why the federal government - a signatory to the Pretoria agreement, the issuer of the interim administration's founding regulation and the approver of the interim administration's president - has remained silent is much discussed. However, as clearly stated in Proclamation No. 359/95, which determined the circumstances under which the federal government intervenes in regional affairs, it is stipulated that the federal government and the House of Federation have a high responsibility towards a region in which an interim administration has been established. Article 16 of Proclamation 359/95 stipulates the submission of reports and follow-up, while Article 17 sets out informing the public.

Under these articles it is clearly set out that the federal government shall periodically submit a report on the interim administration to the House of Federation, and in addition to the government, the House of Federation too has obligations. The proclamation, which stipulates that the Prime Minister shall regularly submit his report and follow-up assessment to the House of Federation every two months, also stipulates that he shall appear and report whenever members of the House of Federation ask him to give an explanation. In addition, it is indicated that the government and the House of Federation must give explanations to the media. Although the law says this, what is observed regarding the Tigray interim administration, both on the government side and on the part of the House of Federation, is a long silence.

a6253.t:
Walvis Bay Hospital has received a N$20 million mobile intensive care unit from the US government.
The fully equipped five-bed Intensive Care Unit is self-sufficient with its own power, water, and sewage systems to allow it to operate independently in the field.
The ICU is also stocked with N$600,000 worth of medicine to ensure its immediate operation.
The ICU is the first of four donations that will be installed across Namibia in the coming months.
"These donations include a second five-bed ICU in Otjiwarongo, as well as two field hospitals in Outapi and Katima Mulilo that include a 30-bed Negative Pressure Isolation Facility and a UN Level 1 Urgent Care Clinic. These donations will total over N$128 million in value and represent the largest single humanitarian assistance donation to date to the Namibian people," says the US Embassy's Acting Deputy Chief of Mission, Tiffany Miller.
The Health and Social Services Ministry has been enhancing the ICU capacity at public health facilities, and the donation is considered a boost in the government's quest.
Its Executive Director, Ben Nangombe, says the ministry discovered during the COVID-19 pandemic that there were only 23 ICU beds in public hospitals across Namibia.
"With the installation of ICU capacity here, it means that instead of having to refer patients from here to Windhoek, they can be treated here. There is a risk when you have to transport a patient who needs ICU care, put them in an ambulance that is not fully adequate, and send them on a long trip on a bumpy road. Anything can happen there, so the best is to provide the service locally, and that's what we are trying to do here with the donation."
To further address the shortfall in ICU beds, the ministry has decided to install ICUs in all 34 district hospitals in the country, and the initiative will be funded by the government.
Nangombe indicated that the mobile ICU will further boost the skills and knowledge of the workforce as they decentralise the service to the patients.

a6292.t:
La Nation Bénin...
En Afrique de l’Ouest, l’accès au financement demeure un
défi majeur pour les petites et moyennes entreprises et freine la croissance et
l’innovation. Face à la frilosité du secteur bancaire, les fonds de garantie
s’imposent comme des instruments stratégiques, partageant le risque de crédit
et ouvrant de nouvelles perspectives de financement des projets.
« Le continent africain est potentiellement riche mais
chroniquement sous-financé parce que les institutions bancaires classiques sont
frileuses dans l’octroi des crédits productifs », constate Dr Nguéto Tiraïna
Yambaye, directeur général du Fonds africain de garantie et de coopération
économique (Fagace). Cet avis est partagé par Jules Ngankam, directeur général
du Groupe African Guarantee Fund (Agf) qui affirme : 
« Malgré l’importance reconnue à l’échelle internationale
des Pme, les petites entreprises africaines font face à des difficultés pour
accéder au financement dans leur besoin de croissance et d’innovation».
En Afrique subsaharienne, la faiblesse des cadres juridiques, la volatilité économique et l’absence de garanties bancables aggravent le problème. En moyenne, les dépôts bancaires représentent moins de 20 % du Pib dans plusieurs pays ouest-africains, contre plus de 40 % en Asie ou en Amérique latine (Banque mondiale, World Development Indicators 2024). Cette faible mobilisation de l’épargne formelle limite la capacité des banques à financer l’économie réelle.
Les fonds de garantie permettent aux banques de réduire le risque associé aux crédits accordés aux petites et moyennes entreprises (Pme). « Nos interventions sont à 80 % à l’endroit des Pme », explique Dr Yambaye, rappelant que le Fagace, pour sa part, met en place des lignes de garantie et accompagne les porteurs de projets dans l’élaboration de leurs business plans. « Notre rôle est de pousser les banques à contribuer au développement, notamment dans les secteurs qu’elles évitent souvent, comme l’agriculture et l’élevage », insiste-t-il.
Mécanismes au service des économies
Les dispositifs de garantie présentent de multiples
avantages. Ils permettent d’atténuer les créances douteuses, d’améliorer la
trésorerie des banques en cas d’impayés et de réduire les besoins en fonds
propres pour couvrir les risques de crédit. Ils offrent également un effet de
levier pour stimuler les échanges commerciaux, la création d’emplois et l’inclusion
financière, contribuant ainsi à une croissance durable.
Ces mécanismes permettent de renforcer l’accès au crédit
des petites et moyennes entreprises et industries (Pme/Pmi) et de soutenir des
projets dans les secteurs clés comme les Btp, l’agro-industrie ou l’innovation.
Entre 2021 et 2024, le Fagace dont siège se trouve au Bénin a porté ses
engagements cumulés à plus de 1 300 milliards de F Cfa, avec plus de 4 000
milliards mobilisés et ce, malgré un environnement difficile.
Comme le Fagace, l’Agf permet de lever les freins au
financement des Pme, se positionnant comme un relais indispensable auprès des
institutions financières. «Agf est le chaînon manquant pour permettre aux
banques de réaliser efficacement leurs stratégies de financement des Pme», affirme
Jules Ngankam.
Pendant la pandémie de Covid-19, par exemple, l’Agf a mis
en place un mécanisme de garanties en partenariat avec l’agence américaine
Usaid, mobilisant jusqu’à 160 millions de dollars au bénéfice de 3 000 Pme en
Afrique de l’Ouest. Des accords de garantie de portefeuille, notamment avec
Vista Bank, ont renforcé l’écosystème régional et stimulé les investissements
privés.
Pour sa part, le Fonds de solidarité africain (Fsa)
oeuvre, à travers son plan stratégique «New Frontier 2025 », à diversifier ses
instruments. Sous l’impulsion de son directeur général, Abdourahmane Diallo, le
Fsa élargit ses interventions à toutes les étapes de vie des entreprises :
création, extension, refinancement ou modernisation. « Déterminé, engagé et
responsable, le Fonds s’attache à construire ensemble, avec ses partenaires, un
avenir meilleur et durable », souligne M. Diallo.
Des défis persistants
Malgré les avancées, les dispositifs de garantie en
Afrique de l’Ouest se heurtent à plusieurs limites structurelles qui freinent
leur impact sur le financement de l’économie. Ainsi, les Pme qui constituent
plus de 80 % du tissu économique africain selon la Bad, continuent d’accéder
difficilement au crédit, tandis que le secteur agricole, moteur de nombreuses économies,
reste chroniquement sous-financé.
Le premier obstacle demeure le faible niveau de
bancarisation et d’inclusion financière. Selon la Banque mondiale (Global
Findex 2025), environ 58 % des adultes en Afrique subsaharienne possédaient un
compte bancaire ou mobile money en 2024, contre 
34 % en 2014. Une progression significative, mais qui
laisse encore près de la moitié de la population en marge des services
financiers formels. Cette faible inclusion limite la mobilisation de l’épargne
domestique et prive les banques de ressources longues.
A cela s’ajoutent d’autres défis à savoir déficit
d’information des Pme sur les mécanismes de garantie, exclusion des zones
rurales, faiblesse des capacités institutionnelles de certains fonds. 
Pour y répondre, experts et institutions plaident pour le
renforcement de la coopération régionale, afin de favoriser les synergies entre
les différents fonds de garantie et maximiser leur impact. Il importe aussi
d’accroître la capitalisation des fonds, investir dans la formation et
développer des programmes de sensibilisation.
En surmontant ces obstacles, les fonds de garantie pourront jouer pleinement leur rôle structurant, celui de partager le risque avec les banques, stimuler l’investissement productif et catalyser une croissance inclusive et durable en Afrique de l’Ouest.
a6292.en:
La Nation Benin...

In West Africa, access to financing remains a major challenge for small and medium-sized enterprises and holds back growth and innovation. Faced with the caution of the banking sector, guarantee funds are emerging as strategic instruments, sharing credit risk and opening new prospects for project financing.

"The African continent is potentially rich but chronically underfinanced, because classical banking institutions are cautious in granting productive credit," observes Dr Ngueto Tiraina Yambaye, director general of the African Guarantee and Economic Cooperation Fund (Fagace). This view is shared by Jules Ngankam, director general of the African Guarantee Fund (AGF) Group, who states:

"Despite the internationally recognised importance of SMEs, small African businesses face difficulties in accessing financing for their growth and innovation needs."

In sub-Saharan Africa, weak legal frameworks, economic volatility and the absence of bankable collateral aggravate the problem. On average, bank deposits represent less than 20% of GDP in several West African countries, compared with more than 40% in Asia or Latin America (World Bank, World Development Indicators 2024). This weak mobilisation of formal savings limits banks' capacity to finance the real economy.

Guarantee funds allow banks to reduce the risk associated with credit granted to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). "Our interventions are 80% directed at SMEs," explains Dr Yambaye, recalling that Fagace, for its part, sets up guarantee lines and supports project promoters in drawing up their business plans. "Our role is to push banks to contribute to development, particularly in the sectors they often avoid, such as agriculture and livestock," he insists.

Mechanisms serving economies

Guarantee schemes offer multiple advantages. They make it possible to mitigate doubtful debts, improve banks' cash position in the event of non-payment and reduce own-funds requirements to cover credit risks. They also offer leverage to stimulate trade, job creation and financial inclusion, thus contributing to sustainable growth.

These mechanisms strengthen access to credit for small and medium-sized enterprises and industries (SMEs/SMIs) and support projects in key sectors such as construction and public works, agro-industry and innovation. Between 2021 and 2024, Fagace, whose headquarters are in Benin, raised its cumulative commitments to more than 1,300 billion CFA francs, with more than 4,000 billion mobilised, and this despite a difficult environment.

Like Fagace, AGF helps remove the obstacles to SME financing, positioning itself as an indispensable relay with financial institutions. "AGF is the missing link that allows banks to carry out their SME financing strategies effectively," states Jules Ngankam.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, for example, AGF set up a guarantee mechanism in partnership with the American agency USAID, mobilising up to $160 million for the benefit of 3,000 SMEs in West Africa. Portfolio guarantee agreements, notably with Vista Bank, strengthened the regional ecosystem and stimulated private investment.

For its part, the African Solidarity Fund (FSA) is working, through its "New Frontier 2025" strategic plan, to diversify its instruments. Under the impetus of its director general, Abdourahmane Diallo, the FSA is extending its interventions to all stages of a company's life: creation, expansion, refinancing or modernisation. "Determined, committed and responsible, the Fund is striving to build together, with its partners, a better and sustainable future," Mr Diallo underlines.

Persistent challenges

Despite the progress, guarantee schemes in West Africa run up against several structural limits that curb their impact on the financing of the economy. SMEs, which make up more than 80% of Africa's economic fabric according to the AfDB, continue to have difficulty accessing credit, while the agricultural sector, the engine of many economies, remains chronically underfinanced.

The first obstacle remains the low level of banking penetration and financial inclusion. According to the World Bank (Global Findex 2025), about 58% of adults in sub-Saharan Africa had a bank account or mobile money account in 2024, compared with 34% in 2014. Significant progress, but one that still leaves nearly half the population outside formal financial services. This weak inclusion limits the mobilisation of domestic savings and deprives banks of long-term resources.

To this are added other challenges, namely SMEs' lack of information about guarantee mechanisms, the exclusion of rural areas, and the weak institutional capacity of some funds.

To respond, experts and institutions advocate strengthening regional cooperation in order to foster synergies among the different guarantee funds and maximise their impact. It is also important to increase the funds' capitalisation, to invest in training and to develop awareness-raising programmes.

By overcoming these obstacles, guarantee funds will be able to play fully their structuring role: sharing risk with banks, stimulating productive investment and catalysing inclusive and sustainable growth in West Africa.

a6312.t:
Por: Lourenço Gomes*
1. Toponímia e identificação de lugares com história
A preocupação com a toponímia numa cidade permite compreender as denominações de lugares importantes de uma cidade. Assim, um estudo com foco na toponímia contribui para perpetuar memórias coletivas e reforçar identidades locais, não obstante poder carregar significados controversos. No caso do antigo Largo da Igreja, no Centro Histórico da Praia, pretende-se revelar um marco representativo da memória histórica e religiosa neste núcleo urbano.
Este artigo ressalta a toponímia antiga como ferramenta educativa para promover a consciência sobre a evolução histórica e social de lugares. Busca preservar a memória coletiva, fortalecendo a identidade cultural e o sentido de pertença, além de enriquecer culturalmente os moradores e atrair visitantes interessados em novas experiências turísticas.
A tentativa de estabelecer uma relação entre a denominação do lugar referido com a história da desta urbe vem no seguimento daquilo que fez Pedro Dias, renomado Historiador da Arte Portuguesa, ao estudar a Rua Sofia (Dias, Pedro, 1982, pp. 28- 34). Nesse roteiro de Coimbra, contribuiu significativamente para a valorização do patrimônio histórico e cultural da cidade. Na mesma linha, ambiciona-se o mesmo, relativamente ao eixo urbano referido como Largo da Igreja, na cidade da Praia até 1876.
Esse eixo urbano é mencionado num documento publicado no periódico do governo provincial de então, apresentado como «Editaes da Secretaria-geral do Governo da Província de Cabo Verde e Mappa a que refere o art. 1º do referido edital datado de 10 de fevereiro de 1876». Trazia esse mapa todos os eixos urbanos da cidade (praças, largos, ruas e travessas), apresentando seus nomes em duas colunas: numa, referia-se às «denominações antigas» noutra, vinham as «denominações modernas». Na sua toponímia «moderna» o espaço passou a designar-se «largo do Sá da Bandeira» (B. O. do Governo Provincial nº 7/1876, pp. 35-36).
2. Uma tradição enraizada
A tradição de se denominar ruas, largos e praças está profundamente enraizada na história e na cultura dos habitantes do lugar onde se encontram as modificações que se vão introduzindo nos seus nomes. Persistiu ao longo do tempo segundo a interpretação de Luísa Reis Lima (1992 pp. 211-226), em situações análogas no mundo português. O antigo Largo da Igreja, foi a praça mais antiga, servindo como principal ponto de referência na urbe oitocentista. Por essa razão, foi ali construída a primitiva Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Graça, que deu nome ao local até o final do século XIX. Como todos os espaços em redor do edifício religioso na tradição urbanística portuguesa, o velho Largo da Igreja no mencionado espaço citadino, referenciado numa fotografia de inícios do Século XX como Praça Sá da Bandeira (in Álbum nº 8 – fotografias da ilha de Santiago, foto nº 21- Museu do IAHN-CV), tornou-se num local privilegiado de convivência social, como se pode observar na estrutura dessa praça, no seu ordenamento urbano de então.
Também foi um espaço que para si atraiu outras construções de referência local. Entre elas, destaca-se o antigo Palácio dos Governadores que, antes de o ser, foi a Casa Senhorial de António Teodoro de Bastos, além de outras edificações públicas e ligadas à elite local.
3. Localização no passado da «Igrejinha» de Nossa Senhora da Graça da Praia
As referências que dispomos sobre a localização da primitiva Igreja de Nossa Senhora da Graça, apontam para a existência dessa «Igrejinha», desde inícios do século XVIII. Foi edificada e demolida no local onde, no final do século XIX, foi construído o antigo edifício da Junta do Comércio Externo, até ainda hoje de pé e que alberga o Ministério da Administração Interna de Cabo Verde. O complexo religioso a que se acrescentou a dimensão funerária, como de resto acontecia junto às Igrejas, incluía uma área para sepulturas que se estendia até as traseiras do Paços do Concelho. António Correia e Silva (1998, p. 53) alude ao «cemitério» adjacente à Igreja, testemunhando esta localização. Acerca do local onde situavam tais sepulturas, em ata da sessão de 6 de agosto de 1874 do Concelho da Praia, reportava-se a um terreno por trás do Paços de Concelho, onde na altura, ia ser ampliado os espaços da Câmara. Em dado momento da narração feita na referida ata, chamou-se a atenção, para que se levasse em consideração a medida das covas nos trabalhos das fundações que deveriam ser feitas, nesse local. Chelmicki (1821, pp. 70-72) identificava, na época, o local como um sítio aberto, próximo da igreja onde se enterravam os mortos.
Infelizmente, nada restou da primitiva igrejinha de Nossa Senhora da Graça à qual se deveu a designação de Largo da Igreja, o espaço em frente ao Palácio dos Governadores. Existem, no entanto, referências documentais sobre a mesma e acerca do mais remoto edifício sacro da Praia – a Ermida, também sem referências materiais à qual refere Santa Rita Vieira (1993, p. 26) nestes termos, «(…) uma ermida em que se venerava a Santa Virgem com essa invocação e que ainda em princípios do século XVIII se via no sopé do monte do sítio», ou seja, do planalto histórico onde evoluiu a vila e a cidade.
Em jeito de conclusão…é bom conhecer para valorizar!
O marco toponímico da cidade que temos vindo a ressaltar e que representou durante muito tempo, a simbologia de Nossa Senhora da Graça, a mais antiga padroeira da Praia merece ser conhecido, no momento em que vai ser celebrado mais um aniversário desta urbe (29 de abril de 1858 – 29 de abril de 2025). É essencial que se prossiga com pesquisas e divulgação, a fim de preservar sua memória junto da comunidade. Uma sinalização no local original dessa antiga Igreja fará sentido, como símbolo da fé católica, além de também poder referenciar o evento religioso pouco conhecido entre nós – a eucaristia nela dirigida pelo Bispo D. Joaquim, durante sua visita pastoral ao deslocar-se da sede do Bispado em São Nicolau a Santiago, no ano de 1866.
Sugere-se igualmente uma forma interessante de perpetuar a memória deste espaço, no momento em que vai ser apresentado o Livro: «Urbe, Memória e Crítica da Arte» da nossa autoria. Esta obra, ora editada em 2ª Edição, traz entre outros elementos de memória (histórica e arquitetónica) da Praia Oitocentista, referências importantes da antiga edificação religiosa mencionada. O evento vai acontecer no dia 24 de abril pelas 17 horas, na sede da Uni-Sénior, em Achada de Santo António, situada junto ao Ministério da Família, Inclusão e Desenvolvimento Social. Serão apresentadores do Livro, a Prof. Ângela Veiga e o Arq. Job Amado. No ato, estaremos a propor publicamente que seja identificado o espaço de diversão infantil existente no local para atribuir o nome «Parque da Igreja», fazendo acompanhar à respetiva placa um texto e competente mapa histórico, permitindo desta forma à comunidade, compartilhar memórias e histórias relacionadas com aquele espaço religioso a que muito se deve a fé católica que se consolidou posteriormente nesta urbe.
Referências
Ata da sessão de 6 de agosto de 1874 do Concelho da Praia. Acessível no IAHN, CMP, Livro B2 – (R), A1/7 (1871 – 1900), fls. 46 – 46v.
B. O. do Governo Geral da Província de Cabo Verde nº 7/1876. Praia: Imprensa Nacional.
Chelmicki, José Conrado Carlos de (1821). Corografia Cabo-Verdiana ou Descrição Geográfico-Histórica da Província das Ilhas de Cabo Verde, Tomo I, Typ. de L. C. da Cunha, Lisboa.
Correia e Silva, António (1998). Espaços Urbanos de Cabo Verde, o tempo das Cidades Porto Lisboa: CNCDP.
Dias, Pedro (1982). Roteiro de Coimbra 3. In: Revista Mundo da Arte nº 6, Coimbra.
Fragmentos nº 9-10, maio de 1993. Revista de letras artes e cultura. Praia, Ministério da Cultura.
Lima, Luísa Reis (1992). A rua do Campo Alegre. In: Revista de Ciências históricas. Porto: Universidade Portucalense Infante D. Henrique.
*Ph.D. em História
a6312.en:
By: Lourenço Gomes*

1. Toponymy and the identification of places with history

Attention to toponymy in a city makes it possible to understand the names given to a city's important places. A study focused on toponymy thus helps to perpetuate collective memories and to reinforce local identities, notwithstanding the fact that such names may carry controversial meanings. In the case of the old Largo da Igreja (Church Square), in the Historic Centre of Praia, the aim is to bring to light a landmark representative of the historical and religious memory of this urban nucleus.

This article highlights old toponymy as an educational tool for promoting awareness of the historical and social evolution of places. It seeks to preserve collective memory, strengthening cultural identity and the sense of belonging, as well as culturally enriching residents and attracting visitors interested in new tourism experiences.

The attempt to establish a relationship between the name of the place in question and the history of this city follows what Pedro Dias, a renowned historian of Portuguese art, did when he studied Rua Sofia (Dias, Pedro, 1982, pp. 28-34). In that guide to Coimbra he contributed significantly to the valorisation of the city's historical and cultural heritage. Along the same lines, the same is sought here with regard to the urban axis referred to as Largo da Igreja, in the city of Praia until 1876.

This urban axis is mentioned in a document published in the periodical of the provincial government of the time, presented as "Edicts of the Secretariat-General of the Government of the Province of Cape Verde and the Map referred to in article 1 of the said edict, dated 10 February 1876". That map included all of the city's urban axes (squares, small squares, streets and alleys), presenting their names in two columns: in one, the "old names"; in the other, the "modern names". In its "modern" toponymy the space came to be called "largo do Sá da Bandeira" (Official Bulletin of the Provincial Government no. 7/1876, pp. 35-36).

2. A deeply rooted tradition

The tradition of naming streets, squares and small squares is deeply rooted in the history and culture of the inhabitants of the place where the changes successively introduced into their names occur. It persisted over time, according to the interpretation of Luísa Reis Lima (1992, pp. 211-226), in analogous situations across the Portuguese world. The old Largo da Igreja was the oldest square, serving as the main point of reference in the nineteenth-century city. For that reason, the original Church of Nossa Senhora da Graça was built there, which gave the place its name until the end of the nineteenth century. Like all the spaces surrounding a religious building in the Portuguese urban tradition, the old Largo da Igreja in the said city space — referred to in a photograph from the early twentieth century as Praça Sá da Bandeira (in Album no. 8 – photographs of the island of Santiago, photo no. 21 – Museum of the IAHN-CV) — became a privileged place of social gathering, as can be observed in the structure of that square and in its urban layout at the time.

It was also a space that attracted other buildings of local importance to itself. Among them stands out the old Governors' Palace which, before becoming that, was the manor house of António Teodoro de Bastos, in addition to other public buildings and buildings linked to the local elite.

3. The past location of the "little church" of Nossa Senhora da Graça of Praia

The references available to us on the location of the original Church of Nossa Senhora da Graça point to the existence of this "little church" from the beginning of the eighteenth century. It was built and demolished on the site where, at the end of the nineteenth century, the old building of the Board of External Trade was constructed — still standing today and housing the Ministry of Internal Administration of Cape Verde. The religious complex, to which a funerary dimension was added, as indeed happened next to churches, included an area for graves that extended as far as the rear of the Town Hall. António Correia e Silva (1998, p. 53) alludes to the "cemetery" adjacent to the Church, attesting to this location. As to the place where such graves were located, the minutes of the session of 6 August 1874 of the Praia Council referred to a plot behind the Town Hall, where at the time the Council's premises were to be enlarged. At a given moment in the account given in those minutes, attention was drawn to the need to take into account the measurement of the graves in the foundation works that were to be carried out at that site. Chelmicki (1821, pp. 70-72) identified the place, at the time, as an open site, close to the church, where the dead were buried.

Unfortunately, nothing remains of the original little church of Nossa Senhora da Graça, to which the space in front of the Governors' Palace owed its designation of Largo da Igreja. There are, however, documentary references to it and to the most remote sacred building of Praia — the Hermitage, also without material traces, to which Santa Rita Vieira (1993, p. 26) refers in these terms: "(...) a hermitage in which the Holy Virgin was venerated under that invocation and which was still to be seen at the beginning of the eighteenth century at the foot of the hill of the site", that is, of the historic plateau on which the town and the city developed.

By way of conclusion... it is good to know in order to value!

The city's toponymic landmark that we have been highlighting, and which for a long time represented the symbolism of Nossa Senhora da Graça, the oldest patron saint of Praia, deserves to be known, at a moment when yet another anniversary of this city is to be celebrated (29 April 1858 – 29 April 2025). It is essential that research and dissemination continue, in order to preserve its memory within the community. Signage at the original site of that old Church would make sense, as a symbol of the Catholic faith, and could also commemorate a religious event little known among us — the Eucharist celebrated there by Bishop D. Joaquim, during his pastoral visit when he travelled from the seat of the Bishopric in São Nicolau to Santiago, in the year 1866.

An interesting way of perpetuating the memory of this space is also suggested, at the moment when the book "Urbe, Memória e Crítica da Arte", of our own authorship, is to be presented. This work, now published in a 2nd edition, contains, among other elements of the (historical and architectural) memory of nineteenth-century Praia, important references to the old religious building mentioned. The event will take place on 24 April at 5 p.m., at the headquarters of Uni-Sénior, in Achada de Santo António, located next to the Ministry of Family, Inclusion and Social Development. The book will be presented by Prof. Ângela Veiga and the architect Job Amado. At the event, we shall be proposing publicly that the children's play area existing at the site be identified so as to be given the name "Parque da Igreja" (Church Park), accompanied on the respective plaque by a text and a competent historical map, thereby allowing the community to share memories and stories related to that religious space, to which much is owed of the Catholic faith that subsequently took hold in this city.

References

Minutes of the session of 6 August 1874 of the Praia Council. Available at the IAHN, CMP, Book B2 – (R), A1/7 (1871–1900), fols. 46–46v.
Official Bulletin of the General Government of the Province of Cape Verde no. 7/1876. Praia: Imprensa Nacional.
Chelmicki, José Conrado Carlos de (1821). Corografia Cabo-Verdiana ou Descrição Geográfico-Histórica da Província das Ilhas de Cabo Verde, Volume I, Typ. de L. C. da Cunha, Lisbon.
Correia e Silva, António (1998). Espaços Urbanos de Cabo Verde, o tempo das Cidades Porto. Lisbon: CNCDP.
Dias, Pedro (1982). Roteiro de Coimbra 3. In: Revista Mundo da Arte no. 6, Coimbra.
Fragmentos no. 9-10, May 1993. Journal of letters, arts and culture. Praia, Ministry of Culture.
Lima, Luísa Reis (1992). A rua do Campo Alegre. In: Revista de Ciências históricas. Porto: Universidade Portucalense Infante D. Henrique.

*Ph.D. in History

a6364.t:
- The Program for the Development of Sustainable Livelihoods for Communities in the Sustainable Development Zone of Gorongosa National Park (SLDP Gorongosa) has been recently launched.
- The program has funding of 20 million Euros and will run for five years (2022-2027) and should cover 45,000 direct beneficiaries. 15,000 will be Family Sector Producers and 30,000 will be members of communities reached by awareness campaigns on matters of nutrition, WASH and SRHR.
The Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Mozambique, in partnership with the Gorongosa Restoration Project (GRP), officially launched, on the 23rd of November, the Program for the Development of Sustainable Livelihoods for Communities in the Sustainable Development Zone of Gorongosa National Park (SLDP Gorongosa). The implementation of the SLDP Gorongosa will be carried out by the GRP, with the NGOs Right To Play (RTP) and Resilience BV, through its subsidiary Resiliência Moçambique Lda, as partners.
The SLDP Gorongosa aims to contribute to the improvement of the socioeconomic conditions of the communities in the PNG Sustainable Development Zone, through the implementation of interventions that contribute to the increase of agricultural production, the improvement of nutrition indices, the supply of quality water and basic sanitation of the environment, as well as sexual and reproductive health promotion initiatives. The program, with a special focus on women and young people, covers the districts of Cheringoma, Dondo, Gorongosa, Maringué, Muanza and Nhamatanda and will also contribute to reforestation and biodiversity conservation, thus forming part of the Mozambique Government’s Development agenda.
The program has funding of 20 million Euros and will run for five years (2022-2027) and should cover 45,000 direct beneficiaries. 15,000 will be Family Sector Producers and 30,000 will be members of communities reached by awareness campaigns on matters of nutrition, WASH and SRHR.
The Ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Elsbeth Akkerman, present at the event stated that “the Dutch Government’s development strategy is based on the following pillars: Sustainable Development, Gender Equality, Youth Support, Food Security, Water and Climate and all of them are clearly aligned with the development strategy of the Government of Mozambique”.
On behalf of the GRP, Mike Marchington, Director of Finance & Planning, stated that “the Program we launched today is yet another affirmation of our commitment to combine conservation and community development. Biodiversity protection, to be successful, must be an inclusive process, with the participation of all, where community participation must result in tangible benefits for them, making communities the greatest guardians of the ecosystem. Finally, we want to state that, as a team, we are committed to the objectives of this program and to the rational use of the resources allocated to the SLDP by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands”.
At the end of the ceremony, the Secretary of State for the Province of Sofala, Stella da Graça Pinto Zeca, affirmed the Government’s commitment to the success of the Program, recognizing that the Program is part of the Government’s Plan and the Sustainable Development Objectives of the United Nations that the Government of Mozambique has ratified.
About the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Mozambique:
The Netherlands works to make the world safer and more stable, with less poverty and inequality. It does this through development cooperation aimed at promoting fair and sustainable economic growth and the search for international solutions to conflicts, climate change and resource scarcity. Sofala Province is one of our main focus regions (along with Manica and Cabo Delgado), particularly with regard to Water and Sanitation, Food and Nutrition Security, Gender Equality, Youth Support and SRHR/Health.
About Right to Play (RTP)
RTP is an international non-governmental development and humanitarian organization with the mission to protect, educate and empower children and young people to overcome the adversities of poverty, illiteracy, inequality, disease and conflicts in disadvantaged communities, through the transformative power of the game. Using gender-responsive game-based learning, RTP uses games to challenge harmful gender norms, improve quality and access to education, support child protection, promote psychosocial well-being, and improve health and well-being of children and young people. RTP is an NGO registered in Mozambique since 2002 and in the Netherlands RTP since 2004, based in Canada and implements programs for 2.3 million children and young people in 15 countries.
About Resilience
Resilience Bv is an international network organization with experience in the implementation of Agricultural Development, Irrigation, Information Systems and Remote Sensing projects in development contexts. Through its subsidiary Resiliência Moçambique Lda, located in the city of Chimoio, founded in 2011, Resilência has a deep understanding of agricultural change processes and value chains (including the needs, preferences, aspirations and gender behaviour of rural actors) in Mozambique. Its activities are focused on the water-agri-food nexus and include consultancy, research, project management and implementation, policy support in hydrology, irrigation, agricultural development and remote monitoring. Resilience Bv has its headquarters in the Netherlands and offices in Mozambique, Ghana, Myanmar, Rwanda, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Ivory Coast and Angola.
About the Gorongosa Project:
Gorongosa National Park (GNP) in Mozambique is perhaps Africa’s greatest wildlife restoration story. In 2008, a 20- year Public-Private Partnership was established for the joint management of GNP between the Government of Mozambique and the Carr Foundation (Gorongosa Project), a US nonprofit organization. In 2018, the Government of Mozambique signed an extension of the joint management agreement for another 25 years. By adopting a 21st Century conservation model of balancing the needs of wildlife and people, Gorongosa is protecting and saving this beautiful wilderness, returning it to its rightful place as one of Africa’s greatest national parks
GNP has been described as one of the most diverse parks on Earth, covering a vast expanse of 400,000 hectares. In recent years, the Gorongosa Project, with the support of Mozambique’s National Administration of Conservation Areas (ANAC), has ensured the protection of a recovering population of lions in this system, successfully reduced key threats, and has been recognized as one of National Geographic’s “Last Wild Places” and by TIME Magazine as one of the “World’s Greatest Places – 2019”.
The Gorongosa Project works with the central government of Mozambique (Ministry of Land and Environment, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Education and Human Development, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development, Ministry of the Sea, Inland Waters and Fisheries, Ministry of Culture and Tourism ), with the Sofala Province Directorates of each of these Ministries, and the district representatives of each of these Ministries. We work with traditional leaders in community “regulados” (a “regulado” is a traditional governance structure) through Natural Resource Management Committees.
We collaborate with UN-Habitat, the Red Cross and the World Food Program. We receive support and advice from partners such as USAID, Netherlands, Ireland, Norway, Canada, Portugal, EU, HHMI, among others. We work on scientific research with more than thirty universities around the world, including Eduardo Mondlane University, UniLurio, University of Lisbon, University of Oxford, Princeton University and many more.

a6430.t:
Le secrétaire général du ministère de la santé Dr SALAH BANOITA TOURAB et le représentant de l’USAID à Djibouti M. Lloyd Jackson ont présidé jeudi dernier ensemble la cérémonie de clôture du projet EPIC.
Financé par l‘USAID, ce projet destiné à soutenir le ministère de la santé dans la mise en place de la campagne accélérée de la vaccination anti COVID-19 en République de Djibouti.
Pour rappel, ce projet a été lancé en octobre 2021 par le ministre de la santé Dr Ahmed Robleh au palais du peuple.
Ce nouveau projet a permis au département de la santé de mettre en place une stratégie inclusive, structurée autour d’une campagne intensive de sensibilisation et de vaccination en s’appuyant sur l’engagement communautaire. Pour rapprocher davantage l’accès au vaccin à toutes les personnes de plus de 18ans, le ministère de la santé en collaboration avec les partenaires techniques et financiers ont mis en place des sites de vaccination fixes et mobiles à Djibouti ville et dans les cinq régions de l’intérieur.
Ce projet a également permis de recruter et de mobiliser de centaines d’acteurs communautaires qui ont contribué d’une manière générale à la réussite de cette vaste campagne vaccinale contre la COVID-19.
Le secrétaire général du ministère de la Santé Dr SALAH BANOITA TOURAB a déclaré lors de cette cérémonie « plus de 222 292 personnes ont reçu au moins une dose de vaccin contre la covid 19 depuis le lancement de la campagne d »immunisation soit un taux de couverture vaccinale de 42 ,51 % dont 66,71 % d’hommes et 33,29 % de femmes ».
a6430.en:
The Secretary General of the Ministry of Health, Dr. SALAH BANOITA TOURAB, and the USAID representative in Djibouti, Mr. Lloyd Jackson, jointly presided last Thursday over the closing ceremony of the EPIC project.
Funded by USAID, this project was designed to support the Ministry of Health in implementing the accelerated COVID-19 vaccination campaign in the Republic of Djibouti.
As a reminder, this project was launched in October 2021 by the Minister of Health, Dr. Ahmed Robleh, at the People's Palace.
This new project enabled the health department to put in place an inclusive strategy, structured around an intensive awareness-raising and vaccination campaign relying on community engagement. In order to bring vaccine access closer to all persons over 18 years of age, the Ministry of Health, in collaboration with technical and financial partners, set up fixed and mobile vaccination sites in Djibouti City and in the five interior regions.
The project also made it possible to recruit and mobilize hundreds of community actors who contributed broadly to the success of this vast COVID-19 vaccination campaign.
The Secretary General of the Ministry of Health, Dr. SALAH BANOITA TOURAB, stated at this ceremony: "more than 222,292 people have received at least one dose of the COVID-19 vaccine since the launch of the immunization campaign, a vaccination coverage rate of 42.51%, of which 66.71% are men and 33.29% women."

a6605.t:
The Parliamentary Select Committee on Sanitation and Water Resources has lauded Zoomlion Ghana Limited for its outstanding contributions to improving sanitation infrastructure and waste management in the country, following a working visit to the company’s Accra Compost and Recycling Plant (ACARP) at Adjen-Kotoku on Wednesday, April 23, 2025.
Led by its Chairman, John Oti Bless, the committee’s visit formed part of efforts to identify practical solutions to Ghana’s sanitation challenges. The committee members also inspected other facilities, including the Sewerage Systems Ghana Limited (SSGL), which operates under Zoomlion’s parent company, the Jospong Group.
“I am truly impressed by the level of investment that has gone into these major companies,” Hon. Oti Bless told journalists after the tour. “Zoomlion’s infrastructure and operations are not only impressive but evidence that the capacity to manage Ghana’s sanitation challenges already exists.”
The Chairman, however, lamented the government’s failure to meet its financial obligations to service providers, revealing that the state currently owes Zoomlion over GH₵1.2 billion in arrears. “How can a company function effectively without resources?” he questioned. He indicated that the Ministry of Finance has earmarked GHS 13 billion in the 2025 budget to settle debts owed to sanitation service providers and expects swift action.
Oti Bless also advocated for the establishment of a dedicated sanitation fund, arguing that a fixed percentage of the sanitation and energy levy should be channelled into sanitation improvement. “Sanitation is a daily necessity that requires a dedicated source of funding. If 40 pesewas is being raised through the levy, 20 pesewas should go to sanitation,” he proposed.
The MP for Nkwanta North further called for enhanced public education, media partnerships, and enforcement of local sanitation bye-laws. “Many district assemblies' bye-laws are not gazetted, making them unenforceable,” he explained. “We need to fix this and work with the media to launch nationwide campaigns to educate the public.”
He praised Zoomlion’s innovation, particularly its ventures into local production of tricycles, furniture, and waste processing systems. “We urge Ghanaians and civil society to support and buy local products from Zoomlion. This fight is about public health, not politics,” he said.
In an earlier presentation, the Executive Chairman of the Jospong Group, Joseph Siaw Agyepong, called on Parliament to ensure strict enforcement of sanitation and environmental bye-laws. “What we do here goes beyond just cleaning,” he said. “We are tackling cholera, environmental degradation, and even enhancing tourism, all while improving sanitation infrastructure.”
Agyepong also appealed to the government to consider reducing import taxes on essential sanitation equipment. “The work we do often lacks the recognition and support it deserves,” he lamented. “We are currently in discussions about taxes on some of our equipment, and we urge the committee to take up this matter.”
He reiterated the importance of continued support for Zoomlion’s initiatives. “With the right backing, we can achieve much more in improving Ghana’s sanitation landscape,” he added.
As the tour concluded, Oti Bless reaffirmed the committee’s commitment to driving tangible improvements in sanitation. “We have hit the ground running, and we will not stop until the right things are done,” he said.

a6613.t:
Despite billions spent annually, CSR has largely failed to deliver sustainable development. The professionalization of these approaches has not addressed the systemic inequality and injustice in the African continent, it often reflects the resource curse concept.
In many parts of Africa, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has long been touted as a bridge between the continent’s critical minerals and its equally enormous development needs. What began as corporate giving built on philanthropy has evolved into structured CSR, yet the most affected communities remain excluded.
Despite billions spent annually, CSR has largely failed to deliver sustainable development. The professionalization of these approaches has not addressed the systemic inequality and injustice in the African continent, it often reflects the resource curse concept.
The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) supplies more than 70% of the world’s cobalt, a mineral critical for the production of electric vehicles and rechargeable lithium batteries used in most tech devices. Yet, more than 40,000 children work in unsafe artisanal mining sites without access to school or healthcare.
However, with members of the Cobalt for Development and Fair Cobalt Alliance significant financial investments and high-profile sustainability frameworks, companies like Glencore’s impact on communities remain negligible compared to the company’s global business footprint.
Moreover, with over 250 active CSR investors and a 526% growth in value, communities still struggle with poor roads, unsafe water, environmental degradation, and deteriorating public infrastructures.
In Nigeria, the Niger Delta region demonstrates this disconnect. Building on the World Bank’s 2024 global gas flaring tracker and the International Energy Agency’s 2024 global methane tracker, Capterio reported that oil companies flared approximately 267 billion cubic meters of gas in a year, wasting about $48 billion in potential revenues globally. Nigeria, with a flaring penalty in place, only collected about one-fourth of the fees due. It is observed that CSR often functions as reputational whitewashing, prioritizing optics over outcomes. This water bottle CSR program provides branded boreholes and PR campaigns, while affected communities continue to suffer from pollution.
In extractive regions around Africa, the impact of CSR rarely reaches those most affected and in need. A working paper found that CSR funds from mining companies in the DRC, Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Zambia disproportionately benefit local elites. Rather than benefitting the underserved communities, this CSR approach reinforces elite control and deepens the marginalization. A 2022 research found out that Shell’s CSR spent millions on clean-ups and infrastructure projects that had minimal direct impact in Ogoniland but mostly benefitted the local elites behind the scenes. The study concluded that the pro forma version of CSR permitted companies to amplify success while environmental damage and community grievances persisted. In these situations, approximately 5% of CSR budgets are directly committed to civil society organizations (CSOs) and community-based organizations (CBOs).
Big Tech companies also adopt the same extractive logic. The African Digital Rights Network (ADRN) reports that tech giants spend less than 4% of global research and development (R&D) in Africa, considering the continent’s massive user base and data extraction. In 2024 alone, Apple, Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft, among others, spent over $230 billion on R&D. On the other hand, African countries invest only 0.45% of their GDP in R&D, well below the globally accepted average of 1.7%, which mostly comes from foreign donors. This digital colonialism hinders Africa’s capacity to build its digital public infrastructure or participate actively in global tech governance processes, thereby reducing Africans to data points and consumers rather than co-creators of their digital future.
Amidst this, CSOs across Africa are experiencing shrinking access to funding. In 2024, Official Development Assistance (ODA) to Africa declined by 7.1% for the first time in five years. Projections for 2025 are even more appalling, with the African Development Bank warning of a potential $39.84 billion shortfall. Funding cuts by Canada, Germany, the United Kingdom, the United States of America, and the Netherlands expose huge gaps in basic services in low-income countries. With this notable void, CSR and Corporate Shared Values (CSV) positioned as alternatives remain ineffective, lacking community ownership, sustainability, or public trust.
However, Ghana’s community development agreements in mining communities portray increased project success. The Newmont Ahafo Development Foundation (NADeF) generated about $4 million annually to support local communities and has invested over $6.4 million in cultural programs, healthcare facilities, schools, and water systems. NADeF also established Sustainable Development Committees (SDCs) to ensure local participation and accountability. In Uganda, community-managed solar microgrids, backed by local cooperatives and diaspora funding, are sustainably and inclusively lighting up thousands of rural households, beyond donor cycles.
At the policy level, the African Union’s Africa Mining Vision, adopted in 2009, was developed to shift the continent from raw material extraction to value addition and industrialization. The African Minerals Development Centre and the Africa Minerals Strategy Group further this agenda by promoting intergovernmental collaboration. Yet, with $97.9 billion in PPP investment since 2019, Africa still attracts only 7% of global PPP funding. According to the UN Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA), closing Africa’s infrastructure gap requires up to $170 billion annually. To meet this goal, the private sector must move beyond compliance and aesthetics to practically integrate accountability, environmental justice, and gender inclusion into their core business strategies.
Extraction exploits communities, and it does not have to be this way. Evidence shows that LLD can be more impactful in places where CSR is ineffective and unsustainable.
Corporations often claim they are not development agencies, but many benefit from tax and regulatory exemptions and land subsidies. The social license to operate must go beyond PR, it must become a genuine social contract. If CSR is to matter, it must stop being a tool for reputational laundering, led by greenwashing and begin to be a vehicle for locally led development.
The path forward is not to abandon CSR, but to reform it. It means rooting it in local realities, building power for communities, and connecting it with inclusive governance. Businesses that hope to stay relevant in building stronger African societies must initiate this shift. Africa is not a problem to be solved or a resource to be exploited, it is a continent of agency, culture, ideas, and partnership. If CSR is to make sense, it must contribute in building the Africa communities actually want.

a6738.t:
Parliament has approved GH¢10.10 billion for the year 2025 along with a distribution formula to enable the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) to undertake its activities earmarked for the year.
The amount is almost GH¢4 billion more than the GH¢6.87 billion that was allocated to the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF) for its programmes and activities for last year.
The increase has been made possible due to the uncapping of the NHIF by the current government.
The approval followed a closed-door meeting the Committee of the Whole had with officials of the NHIA, led by the acting Chief Executive Officer, Dr Victor Asare Bampoe, during which the House approved the proposed formula for disbursement of the NHIF for 2025.
The proposed formula was presented to Parliament and the Speaker of Parliament referred it to the Committee of the Whole for consideration and report.
Support for dialysis
Per the approved formula, GH¢2 million will go to support needy patients, below 18 years and above 60 years, suffering from kidney diseases and undergoing dialysis treatment.
Besides, GH¢6.56 billion, representing 65.1 per cent, will be allocated for payment of claims in 2025, GH¢1.23 billion, representing 12.3 per cent, will support NHIA operational expenses, GH¢124 million will support NHIA district offices and GH¢984 million will support the Ministry of Health.
Besides, GH¢125 million will be used as support for district health projects, GH¢188 million for biometric ID cards and authentication system while GH¢111 million will be for claims processing centres, among others.
Speaking to the press after the meeting, the Minister of Health, Kwabena Mintah Akandoh, said the increase in budget allocation to the NHIA was in fulfillment of the promise President John Dramani Mahama made to uncap the NHIF in the 2025 budget.
He said in 2024, the amount the formula allocated was around GH₵6 billion and as a result of the uncapping, GH₵10 billion had been allocated to the Fund.
Mr Akandoh said the difference would cater for about three main items, including free primary healthcare, to fill the huge funding gap due to withdrawal of donor support to the health sector.
The other area is support for the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, known as the Mahama Cares initiative.
Under the free primary healthcare, he said any Ghanaians who fell sick could seek free medical treatment in any health centre.
On the withdrawal of the support by the country’s donor partners, such as the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), he said it had created a huge funding gap in the health sector.
“Therefore, revenue to be generated as a result of uncapping the NHIF will go to fill the gap,” the Health Minister said.
Mr Akandoh said a percentage would finance the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, Mahama Cares initiative.
Funding dialysis treatment
He recalled that in the 2024 formula, the government allocated GH₵2 million for dialysis treatment of people with renal issues below the age of 18 years and above the age of 60 years, would be taken care of by the NHIF.
“That formula died on December 31, 2024; so, beyond that there was no policy in place for dialysis. Now, with this formula what we have done is to include dialysis as part of the benefit package of the National Health Insurance Scheme just like malaria or any other disease.
“So, the policy direction is that we are going to fund the dialysis issues in this country,” he said.
That notwithstanding, Mr Akandoh said, Mahama Cares would be dedicated to chronic non-communicable diseases.
“And so any of these diseases that have not been captured by NHIF will then be captured by the Mahama Cares because we all know that about 45 per cent of our mortality is attributable to the non-communicable diseases, and as a country, we need to urgently find a solution to it, especially at this critical time where our donor partners are withdrawing their funds,” Mr Akandoh stated.

a6859.t:
Member of Parliament Emma Theofelus said women face gender biases in legal and macroeconomic frameworks, including young professionals in the informal sector.
Theofelus shared this at a high-level panel at the opening ceremony of the YouthConnekt Africa Summit in Accra, Ghana, last week.
The panellists discussed the opportunities for young people, where The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is concerned, as well as the role of young women in delivering the vision for Africa beyond aid.
The free-trade area is the largest in the world in terms of the number of participating countries since the formation of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
It was created by the African Continental Free Trade Agreement among 54 of the 55 African Union nations.
Accra, Ghana, serves as the Secretariat of AfCFTA, and it was commissioned and handed over to the AU by the president of Ghana, Nana Akufo-Addo, on 17 August 2020 in Accra.
“Africa’s demographic dividend is very much dependent on the full inclusion of women across overlapping political, social and economic spheres,” stated Theofelus.
She said, this has far-reaching implications like limited opportunities to funding from commercial banks, trust from potential clients, fewer employees, as well as lower sales and annual turnover, furthermore constraining young women from starting, operating and scaling up enterprises.
The deputy minister of information, communication and technology (ICT) added narrowing the digital divide will ensure women fully participate in the 4th Industrial Revolution and have access to economic opportunities online.
“Women have, in the past, been deliberately excluded from all the first three industrial revolutions. The opportunities availed by technology today cannot be ignored; the continent needs to take deliberate actions to ensure no young person is unable to use technology today,” she stated.
Theofelus said, for Africa to develop, there needs to be gradual less reliance on the West, through foreign aid that has failed to deliver sustainable economic growth on the continent.
She is advocating for more intra-Africa trade to alleviate poverty amongst other things.

a7025.t:
